teaser.text: Trip.com Group Limited is a travel marketplace: it helps people find, compare and arrange trips through Ctrip, Qunar and Trip.com. To understand its business, follow the money from traveler to supplier, then watch the fees, costs and risks that remain with the platform.

stock.closing: The full Trip.com memo also explains its business, rivals, management and risks.

blocks.heading: Where could Trip.com’s shares be by 2029?

paragraphs.text: The forecast starts at HK$330.34 by October 2027, a 5% total return including dividends, and reaches HK$422.75 by October 2029, a 36% total return including dividends. It assigns 35% probability to bear, 50% to base and 15% to bull. The outcome turns on hotel commissions, pricing and inventory after the July 2026 order; repeat use, direct traffic and contribution profit in international markets; and liquidity around the US$1.5 billion convertible notes, with cash repayment available to holders on June 15, 2027. Conversion, awards and buybacks shape dilution.

blocks.heading: What has to go right or wrong for Trip.com?

paragraphs.text: The bear case starts at CNY9,825 million and ends at CNY11,520 million. It assumes weaker demand, revenue of CNY65.5 billion initially, and margins of 15% before a limited recovery. The bull case starts at CNY16,800 million and ends at CNY22,620 million, requiring margins to rise from 24% to 26%. Q2 revenue grew 6%, while international-platform revenue rose over 50%; however, sales and marketing expense rose 15%, and the reported operating loss included the anti-monopoly penalty.

blocks.heading: How much cash does Trip.com really make?

paragraphs.text: Operating cash flow measures cash generated by the business. Free cash flow subtracts capital spending, lease payments and interest. The “real” measure also subtracts stock pay, which requires no immediate cash but still dilutes existing owners. Trip.com remained strongly cash-generative in 2025, although real free cash flow was lower than in the preceding years.

blocks.heading: What does an investor pay for Trip.com today?

paragraphs.text: The shares look inexpensive on reported earnings, but reported earnings are not the same as recurring travel profit. The trailing P/E divides the share price by recent earnings per share, so a one-off gain can make the ratio look artificially low. Trip.com’s 2025 profit included a RMB15.2 billion gain from selling part of its MakeMyTrip investment. The cash was real, but it came from selling an asset, not from earning more hotel commissions or ticket fees. The higher forward P/E therefore points toward more normal future earnings.

dividend.opening: Trip.com’s latest stated dividend is US$0.30 per share. Free cash flow covers the dividend, while the company also uses cash for buybacks and retains some after shareholder payments.
dividend.closing: The full Trip.com memo also covers its business, rivals, management priorities and the risks around regulation, hotel economics and international growth.

blocks.heading: How much does Trip.com pay shareholders per share?

paragraphs.text: The company has begun returning more of that cash to shareholders. Its November 2023 policy allows buybacks, dividends, or both. In February 2025, the board approved a US$0.30-per-share dividend. It also authorized up to US$400 million of additional repurchases. In August 2025, it authorized a further repurchase program of up to US$5 billion. These authorizations create room to buy shares; they do not guarantee that the full amount will be spent.

blocks.heading: Does Trip.com’s cash cover its dividend?

paragraphs.text: The remaining weakness is visibility. The supplied figures do not separate spending on equipment and software from other operating cash uses, so they cannot show precisely how much cash Trip.com reinvested in its platform. The broad conclusion is still firm: the company used acquisitions to build reach, then used stronger cash generation to repay debt and begin returning capital, while the standalone returns from several major expansion bets remain hidden.

blocks.heading: What has Trip.com guided for the next few quarters?

paragraphs.text: Management guidance is a company’s best short-term estimate, not a permanent promise. In June, Trip.com expected Q2 2026 revenue to grow by approximately 3%–8% year over year. Revenue grew 6%, so the forecast described that quarter reasonably well.

Once Q2 ended, however, the forecast became historical information. In the September results and call, management discussed globalization, service quality, artificial intelligence and compliance, but gave no new revenue or margin target. Its comments therefore describe priorities rather than a quantified forecast.

blocks.heading: What should investors watch in Trip.com’s next results?

paragraphs.text: The central risk is whether Trip.com can change its hotel practices without weakening the economics of its platform.

If hotels can work more freely with rival platforms, Trip.com may lose bargaining power. Commissions could fall, promotional costs could rise or control over prices and availability could weaken. That is why the remedy matters beyond its one-time charge.
